hints: Start from chromium metal, Z = 24, which is the exception $\text{[Ar] }3\text{d}^54\text{s}^1$, then think about which electrons are lost first when the $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion forms.
walkthrough:
Build from the chromium atom then remove electrons correctly**
Think of neutral Cr as $1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^2 2\text{p}^6 3\text{s}^2 3\text{p}^6 3\text{d}^5 4\text{s}^1$. When a transition metal forms a positive ion, the $4\text{s}$ electrons are always lost before the $3\text{d}$ electrons. To make $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ you remove the one $4\text{s}$ electron and then two $3\text{d}$ electrons, leaving $3\text{d}^3$.

Write the full ion configuration**
That gives $1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^2 2\text{p}^6 3\text{s}^2 3\text{p}^6 3\text{d}^3$. There is no $4\text{s}$ left in the ion.

hints: Focus on the two essential parts of the definition: what sits in the centre, and what is attached to it by what type of bond.
walkthrough:
Picture what a complex looks like**
Take $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ as your model. In the middle there is a $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ metal ion. Around it are six water molecules. Those surrounding species are called ligands.

Turn the picture into the definition**
A complex ion is simply a central metal atom or ion with ligands bonded to it by coordinate bonds. You only need to state the central metal plus surrounding ligands to earn the mark.
Final answer: A central metal atom or ion surrounded by / bonded to one or more ligands.

hints: Recall that $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ with $\text{NaOH}$ gives a hydroxide precipitate, with $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ in alkali is oxidised to higher oxidation state, and with excess $\text{NH}_3$ undergoes ligand exchange.
For $\text{NaOH}$, think of $\text{OH}^-$ replacing water and then deprotonating to give a neutral chromium(III) hydroxide solid.
For $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, think oxidation state change: Cr(III) to Cr(VI) as yellow $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$ or orange $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$.
For excess $\text{NH}_3$, think of complete replacement of all six water ligands by ammonia with no change in oxidation state.
Match each change to its reaction type: forming an insoluble solid, changing oxidation number, or swapping one ligand for another.
walkthrough:
Use the cobalt(II) analogy**
You are told Cr(III) behaves like Co(II). That is a strong clue. Co(II) gives $\text{Co(OH)}_2$ precipitate with $\text{NaOH}$, is oxidised by $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, and forms $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ with excess ammonia. Apply the same three ideas to chromium.

NaOH gives a hydroxide precipitate**
$\text{OH}^-$ acts as a base and precipitates chromium(III) hydroxide, $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$, often written as $\text{Cr(OH)}_3(\text{H}_2\text{O})_3$. No oxidation state change occurs, the $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ simply joins with $\text{OH}^-$. This is precipitation.

H2O2 oxidises Cr(III) to Cr(VI)**
Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising agent. It oxidises Cr from +3 to +6, forming chromate(VI), $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$, which equilibrates to dichromate(VI), $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$, in acid. Because oxidation number changes, this is redox, specifically oxidation.

Excess NH3 swaps the ligands**
Ammonia is a good ligand and in excess it replaces all six waters: $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Cr(NH}_3)_6]^{3+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Chromium stays as +3, only the species around it change. This is ligand substitution.

Final answer: With $\text{NaOH(aq)}$: $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ or $\text{Cr(OH)}_3(\text{H}_2\text{O})_3$ ; precipitation.
With $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2\text{(aq)}$: $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$ / $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ ; redox / oxidation.
With excess $\text{NH}_3\text{(aq)}$: $[\text{Cr(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ ; ligand substitution.

hints: Remember that colour in transition complexes comes from splitting of d-orbitals and absorption of part of visible light to promote an electron across the gap $\Delta E$.
Think about what controls the size of $\Delta E$: the identity of the ligand, the oxidation state and the geometry, and how a different $\Delta E$ changes which colour is absorbed.
walkthrough:
Recall where colour comes from**
In both complexes Cr is +2 with d-electrons. Ligands split the d-orbitals into two sets separated by $\Delta E$. An electron can jump across this gap by absorbing a photon where $\Delta E = h\nu$. The colour you see is the complementary colour to the light absorbed.

Link different ligands to different Delta E**
Water and ethanoate are different ligands with different field strengths. They split the d-orbitals by different amounts, so $\Delta E$ is different. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and wavelength of visible light is absorbed, so the transmitted or reflected colour looks different.

Final answer: The energy gap $\Delta E$ between d-orbitals is different in the two complexes.
A different frequency / wavelength / energy of visible light is absorbed, so different colours are seen.

hints: Look at the diagram: each ethanoate bridges with two O atoms joined by a curved line, while each water bonds through only one O atom, so count lone pairs donated per ligand.
walkthrough:
Count bonds per ligand**
Look carefully at the structure. Each $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ uses its two oxygen atoms to bond to two different Cr atoms, donating one lone pair from each O. That is two dative bonds per ethanoate, so it is bidentate. Each water uses only its single O to bond once to one Cr, donating one lone pair, so it is monodentate.
Final answer: Ethanoate ions are bidentate whereas $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is monodentate; ethanoate forms two dative bonds / donates two lone pairs, water forms one.

hints: For one Cr atom, count the total number of coordinate bonds to it: four O atoms from ethanoates plus one water O plus one Cr, then recall which geometry has that coordination number.
walkthrough:
Count bonds and name the shape**
Focus on one Cr. It is bonded to four O atoms from four different ethanoate ligands, plus one $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, plus the other Cr. That is six bonding directions in total, so coordination number is six. Six groups arranged to minimise repulsion gives an octahedral arrangement around each Cr.
Final answer: Coordination number = 6 and geometry around Cr = octahedral.

hints: Remember that in complexes, bonds from ligands to metal and unusual metal to metal interactions in this paddlewheel structure involve sharing of electron pairs supplied by one partner.
walkthrough:
Identify the bond type**
The Cr-Cr interaction in this dimeric complex is formed by donation of electron pairs into vacant orbitals, just like ligand to metal bonds. It is therefore described as a coordinate or dative covalent bond, not a normal shared pair covalent bond between identical non-metals.
Final answer: Coordinate / dative covalent bond.

hints: Write the two half-equations from the Data Booklet: $\text{Cr}^{3+} + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cr}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (or to $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$), reversing the chromium one for oxidation.
Balance electrons by multiplying the $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ oxidation by 4 to match the 4 electrons gained by $\text{O}_2$, then combine and cancel electrons.
walkthrough:
Set up oxidation and reduction**
$\text{Cr}^{2+}$ is oxidised: $\text{Cr}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+} + \text{e}^-$. Oxygen is reduced in acid: $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. (The alternative reduction to $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is $\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$.)

Balance electrons and combine**
Multiply the chromium half-equation by 4 to supply 4 electrons: $$4\text{Cr}^{2+} \rightarrow 4\text{Cr}^{3+} + 4\text{e}^-$$ Add to the oxygen equation and cancel electrons: $$4\text{Cr}^{2+} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 4\text{Cr}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge: $4 \times (+2) + 4 \times (+1) = +12$ on each side, O and H balance.

hints: Use $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{red} - E^{\ominus}_{ox}$ with $E^{\ominus}(\text{O}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}) = +1.23\,\text{V}$ (or $+0.68\,\text{V}$ for $\text{O}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$) and $E^{\ominus}(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+}) = -0.41\,\text{V}$.
walkthrough:
Subtract the half-cell potentials**
The more positive half-cell is reduced ($\text{O}_2$), the more negative is oxidised ($\text{Cr}^{2+}$). So: $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode} = (+1.23) - (-0.41) = +1.64\,\text{V}$$ If you used the $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ equation, $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 0.68 - (-0.41) = +1.09\,\text{V}$. The large positive value shows the oxidation of $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ by air is highly feasible.
Final answer: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 1.23 - (-0.41) = +1.64\,\text{V}$
